commitResults.messageTitle: Level-0: Rename Duke, add greeting and exit
commitResults.messageBody:
The template ships with a bare Duke class that only prints the setup banner and has no chatbot behavior yet.

Level-0 requires customizing the chatbot's name and giving it a basic greet/exit interaction.

The main class is renamed from Duke to Verity, prints a startup greeting, and exits with a farewell msg.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-1: Add echo of user input
commitResults.messageBody:
Verity currently only greets the user and exits immediately on bye; other input entered by the user is ignored.

Level-1 requires the chatbot to echo back whatever the user types until they exit.

Let's add a loop that reads each line of input, echoes it back between dividers, and repeats until bye is entered, at which point the existing farewell prints as before.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-2: Add task and list command
commitResults.messageBody:
Verity currently only echoes back whatever the user types and does not remember anything between commands.

Level-2 requires storing user-entered text and displaying it back when the user asks for it.

Let's add a fixed-size array to hold up to 100 tasks, store each non-command input in it while printing an added confirmation, and branch on the list command to print all stored tasks numbered from 1.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-3: Add mark and unmark commands
commitResults.messageBody:
Verity can store and list tasks but has no way to track whether a task is completed.

Level-3 requires the ability to mark tasks as done, and reverse that status.

Let's add mark and unmark commands that parse the task index from user input and flip a per-task done flag stored in a parallel boolean array, updating list to display [X] or [ ] based on that flag.

Task data is currently spread across two parallel arrays (String[] tasks and boolean[] isDone), with mark/unmark/list all indexing into both together.

Level-3's A-Classes extension asks for task state to be represented by a dedicated Task class instead of parallel primitive arrays.

Let's introduce a Task class encapsulating description and done-status, with markAsDone()/markAsNotDone() methods and a toString() that renders its own [X]/[ ] display line. Verity.java now stores a single Task[] array and delegates to these methods instead of manipulating two arrays in lockstep.

This is a pure refactor: command behavior and output are unchanged, only the internal representation improved, in line with the OOP approach the extension calls for.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add ToDo, Deadline, and Event task types
commitResults.messageBody:
Task list only supports generic tasks with a description and a
done status.

Users need to track tasks with different shapes: todos with no
date, deadlines with a single due date, and events with a start
and end time.

Let's add Todo, Deadline, and Event as subclasses of Task, each
overriding toString() to render its own type tag and date info,
and wire up todo/deadline/event commands in Verity to parse and
create them.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add UI test plan and test-ui skill
commitResults.messageBody:
Manually re-testing console behavior after every change is slow
and easy to skip.

Let's record test cases in test/ui-test-plan.md and add a test-ui
skill that runs each command and checks the output against the
expected text.

This follows the module's AI Guidance to have the AI check its own
work, on top of manual testing.

Deadline and event commands split the input on the literal
markers /by, /from, and /to, matched case-sensitively.

A user who types the marker in a different case, e.g. /By or
/FROM, gets it treated as part of the description instead of
being recognized, so the date/time is silently dropped instead of
being an error.

Let's match the markers case-insensitively so the command works
regardless of how the user cases them.

This keeps the parser forgiving of minor input variation without
requiring users to remember exact casing for the markers.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-5: Add error handling for invalid commands and input
commitResults.messageBody:
Invalid inputs: an empty todo description, a deadline/event
missing its /by, /from, or /to marker, an out-of-range mark/unmark
index, or an unrecognized command, was either silently accepted
or handled inconsistently. An unrecognized command line was even
stored as a plain task instead of being flagged as a mistake.

Users had no way to tell why their input didn't do what they
expected.

Let's add a VerityException class, thrown by each parsing/
validation path with a message specific to that failure, and
catch it once in the main loop. Unrecognized commands now throw
instead of falling back to storing the raw line as a task.

A single checked exception type keeps validation cleanly separate
from command dispatch, and forces every parsing path to either
produce a valid task or a clear, specific explanation.

Tasks were stored in a fixed-size Task[100] array with a manual
taskCount counter tracked alongside it, so adding a task meant
remembering to keep two things in sync, and there was a hard cap
of 100 tasks.

There was also no way to delete a task once added, and the fixed
array made deletion awkward where removing an item would mean
manually shifting every later element down by hand.

Let's replace Task[] tasks and taskCount with a single
ArrayList<Task> (A-Collections), using its own size() everywhere
taskCount was used, and add a delete <task number> command built
on the existing parseTaskIndex helper so it gets the same empty/
non-numeric/out-of-range error handling as mark and unmark for
free.

ArrayList's remove(index) handles the element-shifting itself,
so delete needs no manual array bookkeeping, and dropping the
fixed capacity means the task list can no longer silently run
out of room.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-Enums: Represent commands as an enum
commitResults.messageBody:
Commands were recognized with a chain of command.startsWith(...)
string checks, and the same command names appeared again as
literal strings in the invalid-command error message.

String checks for a fixed set of known values don't get any
compile-time safety -- a typo in a keyword, or forgetting to add
a new command to the invalid-command message, would only surface
as a runtime bug, not a compile error.

Let's introduce a Command enum with one constant per command
(LIST, TODO, DEADLINE, EVENT, MARK, UNMARK, DELETE, BYE), each
holding its own keyword and whether it takes arguments, with a
match() helper to resolve user input to a constant and a
describeAll() helper to build the invalid-command message's list
of valid commands from the enum itself.

This makes the switch on Command exhaustive and checked by the
compiler, and means a new command only needs to be added in one
place (the enum) instead of also being hand-added to the
invalid-command error message.
